To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) preoperative coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG) does not reduce the risk of postoperative death and nonfatal MI in any high-risk subgroup of patients undergoing major vascular surgery, and 2) the risk of post-operative death and nonfatal infarct is accurately predicted by a preoperative risk stratification system called the Revised Cardiac Index (RCRI).

The Revised Cardiac Risk index is useful for stratifying the risk of death or non-fatal MI in patients undergoing noncardiac operations and that preoperative coronary revascularization does not reduce the risk of death of non-fatal MI among high-risk subsets defined using this index.
the RCRI is useful for risk-stratifying patients undergoing vascular surgery and that preoperative coronary revascularization is not beneficial in high-risk subsets of the RCRI.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the risk stratification of patients with coronary artery disease who are undergoing vascular surgery.
the development of an accurate risk stratification system to identify high-risk patients undergoing vascular surgery.
the development of new drugs for the treatment of cardiovascular diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
preoperative coronary artery bypass grafting or percutaneous coronary intervention does not improve the outcomes for patients with coronary artery disease undergoing vascular surgery.

preoperative cardiac testing is not indicated in patients with low pretest probability of coronary artery disease who are undergoing vascular surgery, but that preoperative cardiac evaluation and testing are indicated in patients with a high pretest probability of having coronary artery disease who have an intermediate- or high-risk surgical procedure.

there is no benefit of preoperative coronary artery bypass grafting or percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty before elective vascular surgery in patients with multiple risk factors as defined by the RCIR.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
preoperative coronary revascularization does not reduce the incidence of death and non-fatal myocardial infarct in high-risk subsets of patients undergoing vascular surgery.
preoperative coronary revascularization does not prevent perioperative complications in high-risk patients with coronary artery disease who will undergo vascular surgery.
the risk of death and myocardial infarct in vascular surgical patients is predicted by the revised cardiac risk index.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Revised Cardiac Index (RCRI), which is based on the presence or absence of 6 risk factors, is an accurate way of predicting post-operative cardiac complications in patients undergoing major vascular surgery.
patients undergoing vascular surgery are not at increased risk of complications if they are not revascularized prior to their operation.

the Revised Cardiac Index (RCRI), a simple risk stratification score that uses five baseline clinical characteristics, is an excellent predictor of perioperative cardiac complications in patients undergoing vascular operations.
